Aviva set to complete £3.7bn takeover of Direct Line next month
​
Summarise
​
Aviva expects its £3.7billion takeover of rival Direct Line is set to complete next month after 'constructive' talks with the competition watchdog.
The Competition and Markets Authority is not due to report back on its phase one investigation on the takeover until 10 July, but Aviva said on Tuesday it was 'confident' of receiving the all-clear for the deal.
Aviva said on Tuesday: 'Following constructive engagement with the CMA, Aviva remains confident of securing unconditional clearance by the phase 1 statutory deadline.'
Aviva is pressing ahead with plans for a court hearing to sanction a 1 July completion of the takeover, which was first announced on 23 December 2024.
The takeover has also caused concerns among workers at the two businesses after Aviva revealed at the end of last year that around 2,300 jobs would be at risk amid cost-cutting efforts in the wake of the deal.
The combined group will be a sizeable force in the motor insurance sector, estimated to cover more than a fifth of the total British market.
Direct Line owns the Churchill and Green Flag brands, as well as its namesake brand as part of a portfolio offering car, pet, home and other insurance policies.
But the scale of the combined group and its share of the market caught the attention of the CMA.
The regulator announced in May that it would examine whether the deal would result in a 'substantial lessening of competition' in the sector, though the probe was expected given the size of the two firms.
The takeover will see Aviva pay 129.7p in cash and 0.2867 of its own shares for each Direct Line share.
It will also pay up to 5p in dividend payments per share to Direct Line shareholders.
Aviva shareholders will own approximately 87.5 per cent of the new company while Direct Line shareholders will own about 12.5 per cent.
Before the Aviva deal was agreed, Direct Line had fended off a takeover attempt by Belgian company Ageas earlier last year.
Chief executive Adam Winslow joined Direct Line in March with the goal of turning the group around, having been appointed following the ousting of Penny James from the top job.
Direct Line has since announced £100million of cost cuts and axed 550 jobs.
Aviva shares slipped 0.13 per cent or 0.80p to 605.20p on Tuesday, having risen over 28 per cent in the last year. Direct Line shares were up 1.14 per cent or 3.4p to 302.40p, having risen over 50 per cent in the last year.

Aviva unveils wealth push as platform flows reach £4.6bn in 2025
Aviva’s total wealth arm, which includes its workplace pension, platform and advice arm saw operating profit rise 36% to £175m.
Aviva has set its stall out on wealth as its platform net flows increased by 7% to £4.6bn in 2025.
The insurer said the platform momentum was driven by the launch of its onshore bond in the first half of the year. Assets on its adviser platform were £65bn at the end of last year.
Aviva’s total wealth arm, which includes its workplace pension, platform and advice arm saw operating profit rise 36% to £175m.
Aviva’s wealth arm also includes national IFA Succession Wealth; however few details were provided on its performance in the accounts. It also has its direct-to-consumer service which includes Wealthify, the digital wealth business it acquired in 2018.
In the accounts Aviva said its wealth arm is an increasingly important part of its strategy.
‘Since 2022, we have grown [our wealth] assets faster than the market,’ the insurer said in the financial statements. ‘And we’ve improved margins at the same time. In workplace, our profit margin is up by two points over the last two years, making this business a key driver of growth, and a growing contributor to our profits.’
‘We are on track for our £280m profit ambition in 2027. And the importance of wealth within our portfolio is growing. It will soon account for nearly 10% of group earnings, further increasing our share of attractive fee-based income.
Total assets in its wealth division reached £234bn, up 18%.
Aviva saw its best year for individual annuities since the introduction of pension freedoms, it said with sales up 19% to £1.6bn.
The insurer, led by CEO Amanda Blanc, saw an overall group operating profit of £2.2bn. The group also announced a share buyback of £350m.
Aviva’s shares were down 0.16% at 8:40am.

Aviva will use Ukraine ‘playbook’ to mitigate impact of Iran war
​
Summarise
​
The insurer, whose chief Dame Amanda Blanc is in line for a £14m payday as profits jump 25%, has a plan to deal with any inflationary shock from the conflict
Bosses at Aviva will activate their “playbook” from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine if the war in the Middle East fuels an inflationary shock.
Dame Amanda Blanc, the FTSE 100 insurer’s chief executive, said it was too early to say whether the conflict in the Gulf would have a knock-on effect through global supply chains.
The company has “very limited direct exposure” to events in the Middle East but could be caught in the fallout if fighting causes disruption to the global economy. The onset of the Ukraine war four years ago had an “inflationary impact on things like vehicle parts and replacement vehicles”, she said, which in turn pushed up the cost of claims for insurers and fuelled increases in motor premiums.
“We have got a playbook that we utilised back in 2022,” Blanc added. “Obviously if this goes on for a prolonged period of time we would expect that this could have some impact.”
Aviva posted a 25 per cent year-on-year jump in full-year operating profits to £2.2 billion, which included a £174 million boost from the group’s takeover last year of the motor insurer Direct Line, which it acquired for £3.7 billion.
While profits were in line with City analysts’ expectations, Aviva shares, which had risen sharply since mid-February, had slid 19¼p, or 2.9 per cent, to 648¼p by late afternoon on Thursday.
Blanc has won plaudits for reviving Aviva since taking charge of the insurer almost six years ago. She immediately sold off a string of businesses overseas, including its operations in France, Italy, Turkey, Poland, Vietnam and Singapore, to refocus the group on to its core markets of the UK, Ireland and Canada.
This has enabled the insurer to return more than £11 billion to its shareholders since 2020, with Aviva saying on Thursday that it was handing back £350 million through a share buy-back. It also lifted the final dividend by 10 per cent to 26.2p a share, which will return £801 million to investors.

Profits have boomed and Aviva’s share price has climbed by more than 140 per cent under Blanc. However, the insurer said on Wednesday that its chief executive’s pay had “not fully reflected the extent of the transformation delivered”. While she was awarded almost £9.8 million for last year, her biggest package yet, Aviva revealed it was planning to overhaul its executive remuneration policy to increase the annual bonuses and share awards on offer to Blanc and Charlotte Jones, its finance chief.
Under the new pay policy Blanc could take home as much as £14.2 million for this year, if she meets all of her performance targets and Aviva’s share price rises by 50 per cent. Jones, who earned £4.5 million last year, could receive £6.2 million. The new policy requires the approval of shareholders at Aviva’s annual meeting in May.
Blanc is looking towards the next leg of her revamp of the company and said the business was “well positioned” to take advantage of rapidly-evolving generative artificial intelligence models.
Aviva is already using the technology for tasks including claim summarisations in general insurance and complex medical underwriting but is now focusing on “bigger opportunities where AI can transform core areas, like customer service”, Blanc said.
“Most of our claims start on the phone. The plan is by the summer we’ll have a virtual agent able to take the more simple claims calls from beginning to end.”
Asked whether AI would lead to job losses, she said Aviva’s recent expansion meant “any capacity has been absorbed by the growth within the business”.
“As we look obviously to the more end-to-end opportunities as AI scales, then clearly we will look at that.”
Are there good reasons to invest in Aviva?
Another area of growth for the group is wealth management, which Blanc expanded significantly through a £385 million deal in 2022 to buy Succession Wealth. Its wealth division oversees £234 billion of assets, buoyed last year by net inflows of £10.9 billion, and contributed £175 million to group operating profits in 2025. Blanc is targeting profits of £280 million by 2027, which would represent a significant increase on the £88 million that Aviva’s wealth business delivered in 2019.
Don’t write off car cover just yet
Britain’s biggest motor insurers have predicted that a revolution in driverless vehicles is years away and is unlikely to completely upend the market for car cover.
Admiral said in its annual results on Thursday that autonomous vehicles were expected to account for only 4 per cent of cars by 2035, while Dame Amanda Blanc, the Aviva boss, said the Direct Line owner’s “working hypothesis” was that widespread adoption of the technology would not occur before the 2040s.
Analysts at Jefferies, the stockbroker, told clients the forecast from Admiral was “the first prediction by an insurer, to our knowledge” and looked like “a lower penetration than some assumed by the market”. Milena Mondini de Focatiis, the Admiral chief, said the need for the proper infrastructure and regulation would act as brakes on the development of autonomous cars.
There has been speculation that the advent of driverless vehicles will significantly disrupt the motor insurance industry by shifting cover to commercial lines, from personal policies. However, Blanc said that “even with full autonomy you’re never going to get 100 per cent of the vehicles being insured by the commercial lines”.
That was because bad weather conditions and driving in busy cities or on country roads would require drivers “to move between the various levels of autonomy”.
“So our view is you’re always going to need a personal lines and commercial lines insurance proposition.”
Admiral posted record pre-tax profits of £957.9 million, up 16 per cent on 2024.

Aviva´s Direct Line Group fined £10.6m for balance sheet reporting errors
​
Summarise
​
Aviva’s Direct Line business has been fined £10.6 million by the Bank of England’s banking stability watchdog after wrongly calculating the balance sheet strength of its underwriting subsidiary over two years.
The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) said Direct Line’s main underwriter, UK Insurance Limited (UKI), miscalculated its balance sheet during 2023 and 2024 due to “ineffective preventative and detective controls and resourcing issues” across its finance and actuarial operations.
These errors went undetected “for a significant period of time”, according to the PRA, and meant UKI overstated its balance sheet strength to the regulator and the financial market.
The fine was reduced from £21.3 million initially due to Direct Line and UKI’s early admission of the error and moves to resolve the matter swiftly, under the so-called early account scheme.
Direct Line was listed separately on the stock market before being bought last year by FTSE 100 rival Aviva for £3.7 billion.
Sam Woods, deputy governor for prudential regulation at the Bank of England and chief executive of the PRA, said: “We rely on accurate and reliable data from firms in order to be able to supervise them effectively.
“This penalty reflects the importance of firms getting their prudential reporting right.
“Direct Line Group and Aviva’s proactive engagement with the PRA, via the early account scheme, shows how enforcement action can be more efficient when firms are open, candid and accept responsibility for failings at an early stage.”
It was the first case to make use of the early account scheme, according to the PRA.
Direct Line alerted the stock market in 2024 when it found the errors and reported the correct figures.
Bosses at the insurance firm then notified the PRA, launched investigations into the issue and took action to address it.
“Since its acquisition of Direct Line Group in 2025, Aviva has continued to improve Direct Line Group’s finance and actuarial control framework,” according to the PRA.
Aviva said it was “fully aware of this matter prior to agreeing the terms of the acquisition of Direct Line Group and the outcome is fully provided for in the acquisition balance sheet”.
It added: “The resolution of this matter has no impact on the integration of Direct Line Group into Aviva, which is proceeding well, and no impact on the expected financial benefits arising from the acquisition.”

viva fined £10.6m for Direct Line accounting failures
​
Summarise
​
The insurer’s subsidiary cut its penalty in half by volunteering early information on the errors to the Prudential Regulation Authority
Aviva’s Direct Line has been fined £10.6 million by the Bank of England for incorrectly overstating the strength of its balance sheet for more than a year.
The Bank’s Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) ruled that the miscalculation arose owing to “ineffective preventative and detective controls and resourcing issues” in the finance and actuarial functions of Direct Line’s primary underwriting subsidiary, UK Insurance Limited (UKI).
Direct Line first disclosed the accounting error in 2024 as it battled to recover from a string of profit warnings. The motor insurer was later taken over by its rival Aviva in a £3.7 billion deal, which completed the following year.
The business editor’s exclusive analysis of all the latest financial and economic news.
At the time of its discovery the accounting error had gone undetected for a “significant period of time”, according to the regulator, meaning that by the end of 2023 Direct Line had overstated its own funds by nearly £100 million.
As a result it incorrectly reported its solvency capital ratio as 197 per cent, when the true figure was 188 per cent, meaning it had “significantly less headroom”. Solvency ratios are a measure of insurers’ ability to absorb losses and pay future claims.
Independent consultants had previously identified concerns with “financial controls, staff capability, training and resourcing” in UKI’s finance and actuarial functions in 2022 and 2023, including teams that were “overstretched and under-resourced”, according to the PRA.
On numerous occasions staff at the subsidiary were “unable to answer” questions that would be expected in their role. There was also a “lack of knowledge of accounting concepts” and of Direct Line’s own accounting policies.
The consultants themselves also raised as an issue the company’s reliance on external consultancies for support with queries and challenges.
Pressures were further compounded by several “material” commercial transactions in 2023, including a reinsurance deal known as Project Athena, the nature of which had never been undertaken before by the company.
The PRA acknowledged that Direct Line’s senior management had notified the regulator “without delay” after discovering the issue and undertook “detailed investigations to ascertain the root cause of the error”. Several internal reviews have taken place while Aviva has committed to continuing a remediation programme.
Direct Line’s final £10.6 million penalty was halved from about £21.3 million because of its participation in a new voluntary scheme aimed at incentivising early admission from businesses under investigation.
The regulator’s early account scheme offers a substantial discount to firms that provide adequate early information to the PRA and became part of the Bank of England’s enforcement policy in January 2024. It is the first time the scheme has been used in a case, according to the PRA, which described it as a “landmark enforcement outcome”.
Sam Woods, deputy governor for prudential regulation and chief executive of the PRA, said: “We rely on accurate and reliable data from firms in order to be able to supervise them effectively. This penalty reflects the importance of firms getting their prudential reporting right.
“DLG [Direct Line Group] and Aviva’s proactive engagement with the PRA, via the early account scheme, shows how enforcement action can be more efficient when firms are open, candid and accept responsibility for failings at an early stage.”
Aviva said: “The PRA has acknowledged that DLG and, subsequent to completion of the acquisition, Aviva, have co-operated with their investigation in an exemplary manner and, as a consequence, the financial penalty has been discounted by the maximum amount possible.”
The insurer added: “Aviva was fully aware of this matter prior to agreeing the terms of the acquisition of DLG and the outcome is fully provided for in the acquisition balance sheet. The resolution of this matter has no impact on the integration of DLG into Aviva, which is proceeding well, and no impact on the expected financial benefits arising from the acquisition.”
Shares in Aviva were broadly flat in afternoon trading, closing up 1½p, or 0.26 per cent, to 627½p.

Aviva chair: How did I turn us around? I picked the right CEO
​
​
For helping to turn around the insurance company and nearly double its market value, George Culmer is FTSE 100 chair of the year
George Culmer remembers being “half scared” and “half emboldened” after attending his first board meeting more than 20 years ago.
“The scared bit was, ‘Who are these people running this company?’, and the emboldened bit was, ‘If they can do it, I can do it,’ ” recalls Culmer, now 63.
He went on to hold boardroom seats in finance director roles at insurance company Royal & Sun Alliance and banking group Lloyds, but it was not until 2019, after retiring from executive life, that he took his first non-executive position. It was at the FTSE 100 insurer Aviva and one that led to him becoming chairman just 18 months later.
“I didn’t join on any promise [of becoming chairman],” says Culmer, who was immediately thrown into finding a new chief executive after the resignation of Maurice Tulloch and tackling a share price that had slumped to a ten-year low amid calls for the business to be broken up.
He picked Amanda Blanc — now a dame — for the role. An industry veteran, she had joined the board as a non-executive director just four months after him.
“I had not met Amanda before [she joined the board]. It was fortuitous. We did look externally as well, and I spoke to a number of people, but it was obvious to me and the rest of the board that the right call was Amanda, just giving the oomph and clarity of thought to what this business actually needed,” says Culmer.
Within a year, the activist investor Cevian had arrived, demanding a £5 billion capital return. “The thing is to talk and to engage and answer constructively,” says Culmer of dealing with the activist. “I have a lot of time for [Cevian] because they’ve done their homework. They were smart and asked good questions.”
Blanc had already begun to sell off businesses and when Cevian sold out two years later in 2023, the Swedish activist congratulated Aviva on its performance
By the end of 2024, Aviva had regained enough strength on the stock market to make a £3.6 billion bid for rival Direct Line. Behind the scenes, Culmer worked with his counterpart at the bid target, Danuta Gray. “There is a specific role for the chairman in the transaction,” he says, recalling making a call with the introduction: “I’m not ringing up to ask you about the weather.”
For overseeing this transformation of Aviva — one that has led to a near doubling of its stock market value to just under £20 billion, Culmer has been named FTSE 100 chair of the year.
He grew up in a military family and was sent to boarding school. His father had joined the RAF as a private, rising to group captain. His mother had delivered all four of their children by the time she was 25; Culmer is the second born, with three sisters.
“Me and my sisters were the first to go to university,” says Culmer, who recalls feeling “staggered” to get into Cambridge, to read history. “I didn’t really know what going to Cambridge actually meant. I had no idea what I wanted to do because I come from a military background. I’m also short-sighted, colour blind, and a coward — so I couldn’t join the armed forces.”
He became an accountant as it was a “route into what I would define as civilian life”, training at Coopers & Lybrand in London for three years before moving with the firm to New Zealand for two years. He came back to Britain to join the Prudential insurance company, and then spent time in Switzerland at rival insurer Zurich, taking his first boardroom role in 2004 when he joined Royal & Sun Alliance as finance director.
Culmer left there to become chief financial officer of Lloyds Banking Group in 2012 and helped to stabilise its finances to allow the government to sell off the stake it took during the bailout of the bank amid the 2008 financial crisis.
He had never yearned to be a chief executive: “I’ve never put my name forward. I’ve never been asked.” Nor had he taken any non-executive roles until he stopped being an executive: “I was never tempted to do one.”
When Culmer did, he took the seat at Aviva and also at Rolls-Royce, the FTSE 100 engine-maker that has been transformed under chief executive Tufan Erginbilgic. He is also a trustee of the Army Benevolent Fund.
At Aviva, he has revamped the board by appointing seven new directors so that almost half are women. He had to defend Blanc against misogynistic comments at the insurer’s annual meeting in 2022. “One of the things I like to do is make the board as open, as accessible and as informal [as possible], because it encourages people to speak and encourages people to be at ease,” he says.
Culmer also sets out objectives for the board each year: “One of those is always to have fun. You can do dead serious jobs but you have to have fun.”

Aviva burned as more botched green energy gambles turn to ashes
​
Summarise
​
Two more incinerators run by Aviva's investment arm have run into financial trouble after racking up huge losses in the insurer's botched bet on renewable energy.
It comes after The Mail on Sunday revealed earlier this month that a Jersey-regulated 'green' infrastructure fund run by Aviva since 2015 had lost £500 million when three of its other biomass plants went bust.
The controversial projects aimed to generate energy from household waste that would otherwise go to landfill, and were sold to investors, including local authority pension funds, looking for low-risk returns.
But the sites have been dogged by high running costs, technical issues and rows over planning permission.
Investors in the fund have written off £368 million for the trio of plants in Hull, Boston in Lincolnshire, and Barry in South Wales, which collapsed into administration in 2024.
Creditors led by Aviva Investors, who claim it is owed £480 million, are set to recoup less than a penny in the pound.
Now The Mail on Sunday can reveal that one of the fund's other sites, in Plymouth, has been mothballed while another, Hooton Bio near Ellesmere Port in Cheshire, has lost £145 million since 2018.
This includes a £43 million shortfall and debts of £270 million in 2024 - the latest year for which accounts are available. Auditors Ernst & Young only signed off Hooton Bio's accounts on a going concern basis after Aviva Investors said it would not seek loan repayments from the company for a year.
The Aviva director in charge of both the Hooton Bio and Plymouth sites was replaced earlier this month, according to documents filed at Companies House.
Aviva has come under pressure to liquidate its two remaining energy-from-waste plants.
All five facilities are or were majority-owned by an Aviva Investors' open-ended infrastructure fund that is in the process of being wound down and selling its assets, which also included investments in wind and solar energy.
Aviva, run by Amanda Blanc, said the Plymouth biomass facility was being sold to a third party, while there were 'no plans to close' the Hooton site on the Wirral, which the fund bought in 2023. Performance has improved since then with the plant generating enough power to heat about 30,000 homes, Aviva added.
'The fund has generated positive returns for investors since its inception,' a spokesperson said.
'There has been no impact to Aviva shareholders, nor have they suffered a loss.'

Aviva completed £348m in new equity release sales in 2025, a 32% increase on the year before.
The firm said this was driven by higher demand and its launch of a flexible repayment proposition. At the end of last year, Aviva released a lifetime mortgage that rewards borrowers who make repayments on the interest.
Meanwhile, its retirement division, comprising annuities and equity release, saw a 30% fall in sales from £9.4bn to £6.6bn, which it said was in line with guidance. The retirement division also delivered £711m in operating profit, a 5% fall on the previous year.
Aviva saw an 8% decline in protection sales to £345m, which it said was expected due to the consolidation of its propositions in the second half of 2024, following the acquisition from AIG. It said it focused on value over volume, and the protection division’s operating profit rose by 97% to £132m.
Its UK and Ireland general insurance division reported a 27% lift in premiums to £9.8bn, as its UK personal lines premiums rose 50%, supported by the acquisition of Direct Line and growth in intermediated business.
Aviva’s operating profit jumped 25% to £2.2bn.
Amanda Blanc, group chief executive of Aviva, said: “Aviva delivered an outstanding performance in 2025, our fifth consecutive year of strong, profitable growth.
“We have achieved our 2026 financial targets one year early, highlighting the rapid and sustained progress we are making.”
Blanc said the results had been “excellent” across the business and Aviva had been “transformed” over the last five years, adding: “Whilst we have made significant progress, there is so much more to come.”
Blanc said: “Aviva has many in-built advantages, which set us up well for future success, including our unrivalled scale with almost 22 million UK customers, our diversified model and market-leading technology. We have clear strengths in artificial intelligence, which are creating major opportunities to transform claims, underwriting and customer experience.
“We are in a very strong position to deliver long-term growth, especially in the capital-light markets of wealth and insurance, and unlock even more benefits for our customers and shareholders.”

Aviva’s UK and Ireland arm boosts operating profit by 52% and PL growth after DLG acquisition
’We’ve seen huge progress in personal lines – and this speaks volumes about the power of our combined business with Aviva and DLG,’ says chief executive
Aviva’s UK and Ireland general insurance business boosted its operating profit by 52% in 2025 following the insurer’s acquisition of Direct Line Group (DLG).
In a trading update published today (5 March 2026), Aviva said its UK and Ireland arm secured an operating profit of £1.08bn last year, up from 708m in 2024.
This came following growth in gross written premium (GWP), which rose 27% from £7.7bn to £9.79bn year-on-year.
Aviva also noted that UK personal lines premiums grew by 50%, supported by the acquisition of DLG, as well as growth in intermediated business.
When Aviva acquired DLG in mid-2025, it said that the deal “would expand Aviva’s presence in the attractive UK personal lines market, building on its existing strength and creating a more efficient platform from which to serve existing and new customers”.
Following the release of Aviva’s 2025 results, Jason Storah, UK and Ireland general insurance chief executive, said: ”We’ve seen huge progress in personal lines – and this speaks volumes about the power of our combined business with Aviva and DLG.
”I’m pleased to say that our integration is going really well. We’re delighted to welcome our new colleagues on board and it’s been fantastic to see how quickly the teams have come together.
“Across the business, we’re navigating tough market conditions and maintaining bottom line resilience - and that puts us in a really good position for the future.
”I also want to take a moment to thank our brilliant colleagues, our fantastic valued brokers and our amazing customers for their support. Your commitment and collaboration truly make the difference. Here’s to a strong year ahead.”
2026 outlook
Looking ahead to 2026, the insurer said it expected growth and earnings momentum to be supported by its diversified business model and the addition of DLG.
It also felt that it was “well positioned to win over the long-term capturing growth opportunities across our businesses and transforming with artificial intelligence (AI)”.
Aviva said: “We have extensive data assets and a unique advantage through our single customer view.
“We are set to benefit from the investment we have made to modernise our IT estate, with the foundations in place to benefit from AI.
“We have already delivered significant claims indemnity benefits and pricing sophistication through AI models and are seeing early success with claims summarisation and medical underwriting tools.”
Aviva chief executive Amanda Blanc added: ”We have transformed Aviva over the last five years and whilst we have made significant progress, there is so much more to come. Aviva has many in-built advantages which set us up well for future success, including our unrivalled scale with almost 22 million UK customers, our diversified model and market-leading technology.
”We have clear strengths in artificial intelligence which are creating major opportunities to transform claims, underwriting and customer experience. We are in a very strong position to deliver long-term growth, especially in the capital-light markets of wealth and insurance, and unlock even more benefits for our customers and shareholders.”

viva launches £350m share buyback after Direct Line deal boosts profits
Aviva has kicked off 2026 with a statement of intent for shareholders, unveiling a 10% dividend increase and a £350m share buyback programme.

Aviva boss Amanda Blanc: ‘The word relentless will have been used about me’
​
Summarise
​
Head of UK insurer has taken a bold approach to restructuring but must now deliver further growth
Amanda Blanc does not wait for backup. At the start of our interview the video link to a colleague in New York malfunctions and, before technical support arrives, she has leaned over and is prodding the control panel until it springs to life.
Moving fast has become characteristic of Blanc’s style at Aviva, where she has been chief executive for five years. Early in the role she came under pressure from activist investor, Cevian, to make deep cost cuts and improve returns at the UK insurer. She responded by getting deals over the line on tight deadlines and leaving markets where the company would not be a top three competitor. “The word ‘relentless’ will have been used about me,” she says.
After previous bosses built Aviva into a sprawling mix of international divisions, the company’s strength was “being hidden by the noise from other parts of the business”, Blanc explains, so “we removed that noise”.
Out went businesses in markets including France, Italy, Singapore and the US. Within two years, Aviva had sold eight divisions for $8bn, allowing the company to invest and return capital to “long-suffering” shareholders, she says.
Recognising a need to move quickly to provide some gains, given there would be upset among staff about restructuring, Blanc followed up the sales with the £3.7bn acquisition of Direct Line, announced two days before Christmas last year.
“Nobody believed we would complete that deal by the first of July, apart from us,” she says. “But from my experience . . . if things dragged out, if there was uncertainty, that’s bad for both organisations.”
With the Direct Line deal complete — and her deadline met — Aviva is now the largest home and motor insurer in the UK, where it says four in 10 adults are customers, and the second largest general insurer in Canada. The group also offers life, travel and pet insurance and cover for businesses — and Blanc has favoured growth in capital-light products such as wealth and health.
The company has historically suffered from “delusions of grandeur”, says Andrew Sinclair, an analyst at Bank of America, but under Blanc has grown “in areas where it has the right to win, rather than ego trips of past management teams.”
In recent months, her efforts have come good with investors. Aviva’s share price rose to its highest level in almost 18 years in August, after it announced £1.1bn of first-half operating profit, up more than a fifth on 2024. Under Blanc’s leadership, the shares have increased by more than 250 per cent on a total return basis, about four times that of the FTSE 350 insurance index.
“The turnaround in market perception has been remarkable,” says Malik Karim, founder of boutique investment bank Fenchurch and former Tory treasurer, pointing to Blanc’s “judicious use of M&A”.
But while Blanc is deemed to have done a good job at refocusing Aviva and cutting costs, she must now prove she can build on that with further growth.
Her intense approach is somewhat at odds with the usually chummier and slower-moving insurance industry. By sunset, many of her peers can still be reliably found at the pubs around Leadenhall Market, near the centuries-old Lloyd's of London exchange. But Blanc doesn’t drink, she says, and in her time at Aviva has “maybe been out five times for lunch”. Long lunches take “a massive chunk out of your day”, she notes. “I do eat . . . People come in — we’ll have a sandwich.”
One close competitor describes Blanc as being better prepared than anyone in a meeting, including on seemingly trivial or technical details. “You can always tell who’s done the prep work, read the papers — and Amanda always did the reading.”
Others complain her crusading style has downsides. Blanc can be “cliquish”, says one former senior Aviva executive who worked with her. “You’re either in-crowd or out-crowd.” As a result, the executive argues, there has been too little succession planning.
Blanc has shown she can be ruthless when necessary. When restructuring the insurer’s senior ranks after she took over as Aviva boss, she replaced 14 of 15 members of her executive committee.
Later at BP, where she became senior independent director in 2024 after two years on the board, she oversaw the removal of former chair Helge Lund and the appointment of his replacement, building materials boss Albert Manifold. Blanc ignored a suggested shortlist of candidates from activist investor Elliott, and will be held accountable for the choice.
One shareholder describes her as a “no nonsense” executive who is polished and efficient. “She has a reputation for being uncompromising . . . she’s the smiling assassin.” Others have privately grumbled about her lack of oil industry experience. During her time at BP — a rocky period for the company — the board has also faced criticism over its handling of former chief executive Bernard Looney’s departure after he failed to properly disclose relationships with colleagues.
Blanc has more flair than a typical insurance executive — on the day we meet, she is dressed in an emerald green full length jacket with matching shoes and silver jewellery — but comes across as down-to-earth.
Rob Wirszycz, a tech adviser and investor, who served with her on the board of digital claims provider RightIndem, says: “She is very normal. You find a number of people [in insurance] who are a bit precious, but she will talk to anybody and she will listen.”
Blanc traces this back to her roots in the former mining communities of the Rhondda Valley in south Wales. “Because of my background, I don’t have any problem in speaking to anybody in this organisation . . . I can walk into the lift and I can have a conversation,” she says.
Apart from a brief spell in management consultancy, insurance has been the only industry Blanc has known, although she admits this was not the plan when she was a history student at Liverpool university, looking to use her skills at playing the piano and clarinet.
“I was thinking, could I take my piano, my clarinet, my singing, to do something with that,” she says. “I mean, it was completely unrealistic.”
After graduation, she received two offers: one working at Mid Glamorgan county council in Cardiff, close to her parents’ home, and the other in Luton with Commercial Union, which later became part of Aviva.
“I didn’t even really know what Commercial Union did,” Blanc says, adding that she was 80 per cent conscious she needed to leave south Wales and 20 per cent she just needed to “do something different” from her original career plan.
“Within about a few months, I thought, oh my gosh, I love this,” she recalls, crediting the quality of leadership training she was given during that first job. She believes investing more in training managers would boost productivity in the UK.
Does she think about the importance of being a female leader in such a male dominated industry? “You would not ask that question of a man. What I would say is, I sit here today, yet what most people will talk about is that she is one of the nine women in charge of a FTSE 100 company.
“I believe in meritocracy but that is meritocracy across the piece.”
Blanc made headlines in 2022 after shareholders made sexist snipes at Aviva’s AGM. One commented that Blanc was “not the man for the job”, while another praised her and the other women on the board for their skills at “basic housekeeping activities”. She publicly hit back at those comments at the time.
Blanc has also been involved in politics, sitting on two business councils under the Conservatives and advising the current Labour chancellor, Rachel Reeves, on the creation of a national wealth fund. She cites her first meeting in Number 10 among her “pinch me moments”.
Is there another CEO job she would like? “I genuinely think that if you are good at what you do . . . you will be successful, and then somebody will want you to do something else,” she says.
She prefers to stay in the moment. “My advice is: don’t want to be a CEO, want to be good at what you do. I mean . . . it’s a brilliant job. But . . . unless you can be good at what you’re doing now, how do you know you’re going to be good at being a CEO?”

Dame Amanda Blanc declared that “the outlook for Aviva has never been better” last week when she reported third-quarter figures and set out new three-year targets for the FTSE 100 insurer. Is she right and if so, is this optimism reflected in the company’s valuation?
Thrust into the top job in July 2020 after a short stint as a non-executive on its board, the insurance industry veteran has already spearheaded a turnaround at Aviva that has earned plaudits in the City.
Aviva was at a low ebb when she took charge, with investors frustrated by its lacklustre stock market returns under a succession of bosses. This not only streamlined the insurer by refocusing it on its core markets of the UK, Ireland and Canada, it enabled Blanc to step up capital returns to shareholders, with more than £10 billion handed back over the past five years.
It was a pivot praised by Cevian, an activist investor which revealed in 2021 that it was a big shareholder in Aviva and sold out in 2023, when it praised Aviva for having been “transformed from a poorly performing conglomerate to a focused and well-performing insurance company”.
However, despite Blanc’s programme of disposals and capital returns, it has not simply been a strategy of retrenchment. There have been acquisitions too, including a £385 million deal in 2022 to buy Succession Wealth to expand Aviva’s presence in the wealth management market.
The following year Aviva spent £460 million on AIG’s UK protection business and £100 million on Optiom in Canada, while in March 2024 the company announced it was re-entering the Lloyd’s of London insurance market after 24 years through a £242 million deal for Probitas.
All of these deals enlarged Aviva’s capital-light operations, helping it to differentiate it from its more capital-heavy rival Legal & General.
Then came Blanc’s biggest gamble yet, with Aviva’s £3.7 billion agreement last December to acquire troubled rival Direct Line. A further expansion of its capital-light business, the takeover, which was finalised in July this year, makes Aviva Britain’s biggest motor insurer.
Aviva had initially estimated it would save £125 million a year by eliminating duplicated roles, digitising Direct Line’s operations and making other cost cuts following the takeover. As was widely expected, however, it significantly increased its cost synergy estimate to £225 million in its trading update last week, when it also said it expected at least £500 million of capital synergies from the deal.
There was other good news. Even stripping out the contribution made by Direct Line this year, Aviva’s operating profits are still forecast to surpass £2 billion.
The insurer also set new goals for 2028, saying it was targeting a return on equity of more than 20 per cent and aiming to grow adjusted earnings at an average annual rate of 11 per cent over the next three years.
The turnaround Blanc has already achieved has powered Aviva’s share price higher. Its stock closed on Wednesday evening at 632p, up 134 per cent since she was appointed, although it has dipped in recent days amid some disappointment with its third-quarter numbers.
L&G has the higher dividend yield of 9.3 per cent, compared with 6.2 per cent for Aviva, but being close to double-digits suggests investors have questions about the sustainability of L&G’s payout, amid nervousness about its big exposure to the gilt market.

Under Blanc, who shows no signs of planning to move on, Aviva has consistently exceeded expectations, which should give investors confidence it can do the same again with its new targets. However, this is not yet reflected in its valuation.
